meta.title: Atlas of Life
meta.group: Aves I (Palaeognathae and Galloanserae), Aves II (waterbirds and shorebirds), Avialae, Heterodontosauria, Marginocephalia, Basal Ornithischia, Ornithopoda, Pseudosuchia, Pterosauria, Sauropodomorpha, Theropoda I, Theropoda II, Thyreophora
meta.method: Ages, authorities, species and formations from the Paleobiology Database; descriptive data paraphrased from the cited literature and English Wikipedia; scientific articles found through OpenAlex and Europe PMC (data/raw/aves1/papers.json); images from Wikimedia Commons and PhyloPic with their licences. Classification from recent phylogenetic analyses checked against PBDB (docs/TREE_REVIEW.md). Genus list checked against PBDB, Wikipedia and recent literature by the census of 2026-11-27 (data/raw/census/aves1). The volume holds the root of the crown group (Aves) with its two first branches written so far, the palaeognaths (tinamous, ratites and their fossil relatives) and the Galloanserae (waterfowl and landfowl), living and fossil genera, Mesozoic crown birds of these groups included. Living genera that PBDB does not list (no fossil record) are not yet included. Ichnogenera and oogenera are not included.

clades.name: Amniota
clades.sum: Tetrapods whose embryos develop inside protective membranes: reptiles (including birds) and mammals with their extinct relatives.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Amniota, unranked clade), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: Embryo enclosed by three extra-embryonic membranes: amnion, chorion and allantois
No aquatic larval stage; development is direct
Thick, keratinized skin
Breathing by movements of the rib cage (costal ventilation)
clades.notes: Defined as the smallest crown clade containing humans, the Greek tortoise and the Nile crocodile. Amniotes arose from reptiliomorph tetrapods in the Carboniferous and split almost at once into Synapsida and Sauropsida; molecular dates for the split cluster around 310–340 million years ago. Older clawed footprints from Australia have been proposed as amniote tracks, but the claim is disputed.

clades.name: Amorphea
clades.sum: Eukaryote supergroup made of the Amoebozoa and the Obazoa — the latter including opisthokonts (animals and fungi) and their protist relatives.
clades.trank_src: English Wikipedia, “Amorphea”, revision 1382799800 (supergroup; name recommended in 2012 by the International Society of Protistologists)
diag: A fusion of three genes for pyrimidine synthesis (carbamoyl phosphate synthase, dihydroorotase, aspartate carbamoyltransferase) absent in other eukaryotes
Cells typically with two basal bodies, of which only one usually bears a flagellum
clades.notes: Proposed by Cavalier-Smith (2002) as the "unikonts"; renamed Amorphea in 2012 because the supposed single flagellum was found not to be a true shared feature. Its sister group in most analyses is Diphoda (plants, algae and many protists). The internal classification of its smaller lineages (apusomonads, breviates, "Sulcozoa") is still being revised.

clades.name: Archaea
clades.sum: Single-celled prokaryotes forming one of the two primary branches of cellular life; eukaryotes arose from within them.
clades.trank_src: English Wikipedia, “Archaea”, revision 1385819730 (treated as a domain; the PBDB record named Archaea is an unrelated spider genus)
diag: Cell membranes built from ether-linked lipids, unlike the ester-linked lipids of bacteria and eukaryotes
A distinctive rotary swimming organ, the archaellum
Genes and pathways for DNA transcription and translation closer to those of eukaryotes than of bacteria
Metabolisms unknown in other life, such as methanogenesis
clades.notes: First separated from bacteria as "archaebacteria" on the basis of ribosomal RNA (Woese and colleagues). Classification is unstable because most lineages are known only from environmental gene sequences. In the strict cladistic sense Archaea includes the eukaryotes, which branch from within the Asgard archaea; in everyday use the name still means the prokaryotic members only. No archaeal cell fossils can be identified with confidence; the deep record relies on chemical fossils (lipids).

clades.name: Archaeplastida
clades.sum: Large group of mostly photosynthetic eukaryotes whose plastids contain chlorophyll, including green algae, land plants and red algae.
clades.trank_src: English Wikipedia, “Archaeplastida”, revision 1385543025; PBDB record Archaeplastida, unranked clade (no attribution in PBDB)

diag.Plastids: pigment-bearing, membrane-bound organelles, most of them containing chlorophyll

diag: Chloroplasts surrounded by two membranes, consistent with an origin from an engulfed cyanobacterium
clades.notes: Major clades Viridiplantae (green algae and land plants) and Rhodophyta (red algae), plus the minor basal division Glaucophyta. The group also includes heterotrophic lineages such as the flagellates Rhodelphidia and the picoplankton Picozoa, which may be sisters to Rhodophyta; the text places both in a clade with Rhodophyta, called Rhodaria. Some phylogenomic work places a different lineage as closest to Archaeplastida (Yazaki et al. 2022), so its closest relatives are not settled. Sometimes treated as the kingdom Plantae in a broad sense.

clades.name: Archelosauria
clades.sum: Turtles and archosaurs (crocodilians and birds) with their extinct relatives, to the exclusion of lepidosaurs.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Archelosauria, unranked clade), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: Supported mainly by molecular data: about 1,000 ultraconserved genome elements shared by turtles and archosaurs but not lepidosaurs
Recent morphological analyses also place turtles (Pantestudines) inside Archosauromorpha
clades.notes: Named by Crawford et al. (2015). Morphology long placed turtles elsewhere — with parareptiles, outside Sauria, or with lepidosaurs — so turtle origins remain one of the main questions about the group.

clades.name: Archosauria
clades.sum: The crown group of birds and crocodilians: everything descended from their last common ancestor, including dinosaurs and pterosaurs.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Archosauria, unranked clade), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: Teeth set in deep sockets
Antorbital and mandibular fenestrae
A pronounced fourth trochanter on the femur
clades.notes: Defined as a crown group, it splits at its base into Pseudosuchia (the crocodile line) and Avemetatarsalia (the bird line). Many classic features are also found in close relatives outside the crown, such as proterosuchids and euparkeriids, which were formerly called archosaurs.

clades.name: Archosauriformes
clades.sum: Archosaurs and their nearest relatives, such as proterosuchids, erythrosuchids and euparkeriids.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Archosauriformes, unranked clade), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: An antorbital fenestra (opening in front of the eye)
Serrated teeth set in deep sockets
clades.notes: Defined by Gauthier as the clade from the last common ancestor of Proterosuchidae and Archosauria; later definitions use Proterosuchus with archosaurs or with Gallus and Alligator. The group originated in the Late Permian and survived the end-Permian extinction. Many of its members were formerly lumped as "thecodonts", a paraphyletic group no longer used.

clades.name: Archosauromorpha
clades.sum: Diapsid reptiles closer to archosaurs than to lepidosaurs, from Permian long-necked forms to crocodilians, dinosaurs and birds.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Archosauromorpha, unranked clade), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: Laminae (thin bony sheets) on the vertebrae
A posterodorsal process on the premaxilla
clades.notes: Named by von Huene in 1946 but little used until cladistic studies of the 1980s. Main groups: allokotosaurs, rhynchosaurs, Archosauriformes and a polyphyletic set of long-necked forms (Protorosaurus, tanystropheids, Prolacerta); turtles and choristoderes are placed here by some authors. First records are Middle–Late Permian.

clades.name: Asgardarchaeota
clades.sum: Archaea whose genomes carry many "eukaryotic signature proteins"; the eukaryotes evolved from within this group.
clades.trank_src: English Wikipedia, “Asgard archaea”, revision 1385819849 (kingdom Promethearchaeati, formerly the superphylum or phylum "Asgardarchaeota")
diag: Genes for proteins previously thought to be exclusive to eukaryotes (eukaryotic signature proteins)
Histone proteins with N-terminal tails, as in eukaryotes, in some members (Heimdallarchaeia)
Mostly known from environmental genomes; the few cultured members live in close metabolic partnership with bacteria
clades.notes: Its formal name under the prokaryote code is now kingdom Promethearchaeati, with the former "phyla" demoted to classes. Analyses differ on exactly where eukaryotes branch: some place them inside Heimdallarchaeia, a 2025 study places them outside it. The group supports a two-domain tree of life (Bacteria and Archaea, with eukaryotes nested in the latter). The cultured species Promethearchaeum syntrophicum was isolated in 2020.

clades.name: Avemetatarsalia
clades.sum: The bird line of archosaurs: everything closer to birds than to crocodilians, including dinosaurs and pterosaurs.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Avemetatarsalia, informal), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: "Advanced mesotarsal" ankle with a large astragalus and a small calcaneum working as a single hinge
Upright limbs held under the body
Filamentous body coverings in many members, from pterosaur pycnofibres to dinosaur feathers
clades.notes: Named by Benton (1999); also called Pan-Aves. Gauthier's earlier names Ornithosuchia and Ornithodira cover similar ground. Besides dinosaurs and pterosaurs, it includes Triassic lagerpetids, aphanosaurs and other early dinosauromorphs. Only dinosaurs and pterosaurs survived the end of the Triassic.

clades.name: Bacteria
clades.sum: Mostly free-living, usually single-celled prokaryotes, typically a few micrometres long, found in nearly every habitat on Earth.
clades.trank_src: English Wikipedia, “Bacteria”, revision 1385548356 (domain proposed by Woese et al. 1990; PBDB record Bacteria, unranked clade, attributed to Woese et al. 1990)
diag: Prokaryotic cells: no nucleus, and rarely membrane-bound organelles
Circular chromosomes, unlike the chromosomes of animals and other eukaryotes
clades.notes: Once regarded as plants (class Schizomycetes, “fission fungi”), bacteria are now classified as prokaryotes. The 1990s discovery that prokaryotes form two very different groups, descended from a common ancestor, led to the domains Bacteria and Archaea (Woese et al. 1990). Göker and Oren (2024) published the valid names of the two domains and of seven kingdoms of prokaryotes. Bacteria are important in nutrient cycling, nitrogen fixation and decomposition.

clades.name: Bilateria
clades.sum: Animals with a left–right symmetric body built around a head-to-tail axis: more than 98% of known animal species.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Bilateria, unranked clade), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: Bilateral symmetry at least in the embryo (echinoderms become five-rayed as adults)
Three germ layers: endoderm, mesoderm and ectoderm
Usually a through gut with separate mouth and anus
Cephalization: sense organs and nerve ganglia concentrated at the front end
clades.notes: Named by Hatschek in 1888. Traditionally divided into protostomes (now split into Ecdysozoa and Spiralia) and deuterostomes; whether Xenacoelomorpha belong at the base of the group, and whether deuterostomes are a natural group, are still argued. Bilaterians diversified rapidly in the late Ediacaran and Cambrian.

clades.name: Bryophytes
clades.sum: Non-vascular land plants made up of liverworts, hornworts and mosses.
clades.trank_src: English Wikipedia, “Bryophyte”, revision 1385856469 (no PBDB record; monophyly supported by Su et al. 2021)
diag: No true vascular tissue containing lignin
No flowers or seeds
Life cycle dominated by the haploid gametophyte, with a dependent unbranched diploid sporophyte
clades.notes: Most recent phylogenetic studies support the monophyly of bryophytes, while earlier work treated them as paraphyletic and some mitochondrial-based phylogenies do not support monophyly. In the strict sense the name can mean the mosses alone. The text was read on the live Wikipedia page on 2026-11-21 because the recorded revision could not be retrieved.

clades.name: Chlorophyta
clades.sum: Major division of green algae, mostly unicellular, with green chloroplasts and some colonial or multicellular classes.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (Chlorophyta, phylum, attributed to Reichenbach 1834), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: Cells with green chloroplasts bounded by a double-membrane envelope, containing chlorophylls a and b
Cells with a variety of coverings or walls, usually a single chloroplast per cell
clades.notes: Sister taxon to Charophyta (the streptophyte green algae); together they form Viridiplantae. A basal clade, Prasinodermophyta, is proposed alongside them. Most groups are unicellular, but the classes Chlorophyceae and Ulvophyceae show trends toward colonies and multicellularity. Gulbrandsen et al. (2021) restructured Ulvophyceae by phylogenomics, so its internal classification is current only to that revision. The PBDB record attributes the name to Reichenbach (1834), which is not in the Wikipedia citations.

clades.name: Chordata
clades.sum: Animals with a notochord, a hollow dorsal nerve cord, pharyngeal slits, an endostyle and a post-anal tail at some stage of life: lancelets, tunicates and vertebrates.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Chordata, phylum), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: Notochord: a stiff, elastic rod along the body axis
Hollow dorsal nerve cord (neural tube)
Pharyngeal slits
Endostyle, or the thyroid gland derived from it
Post-anal tail
clades.notes: Three subphyla: Cephalochordata (lancelets), Tunicata and Vertebrata; tunicates and vertebrates together form Olfactores. Two conserved protein insertions/deletions are shared by all chordates and no other animals. Tunicates keep the chordate features only as larvae. The phylum name is credited to Haeckel (1874).

clades.name: Deuterostomia
clades.sum: Bilaterians whose embryonic blastopore typically becomes the anus: chordates, echinoderms, hemichordates and extinct relatives.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Deuterostomia, unranked clade), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: The mouth forms at a second opening; the blastopore becomes the anus
Coelom formed by out-pocketing of the gut (enterocoely)
Radial, mostly indeterminate cleavage of the early embryo
More than 30 genes found in no other animal group
clades.notes: Named by Grobben (1908). Lophophorates and arrow worms, once included, were moved to the protostomes by molecular studies from 1995 on. Deuterostome-type development also occurs in some protostomes, so the group is now defined by molecular phylogeny rather than embryology alone.

clades.name: Diapsida
clades.sum: Reptiles that have, at least ancestrally, two openings on each side of the skull behind the eye: all living reptiles and birds and many extinct groups.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Diapsida, unranked clade), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: Two temporal fenestrae (upper and lower) on each side of the skull, at least ancestrally
In neodiapsids, an upper temporal fenestra added to an already present lower one
clades.notes: Some members lost one or both openings (lizards, snakes, turtles) or reshaped the skull (birds) but remain diapsids by descent. The skull-opening classes of older classifications (Anapsida, Euryapsida) are no longer used as groups. Whether the early Araeoscelidia acquired their openings independently of Neodiapsida is under study.

clades.name: Embryophyta
clades.sum: Land plants, complex multicellular eukaryotes with alternating haploid and diploid generations that descend from freshwater charophyte green algae.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (Embryophyta, superphylum, attributed to (Crane et al. 2004)), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: Alternation of generations, with a haploid gametophyte and a diploid sporophyte
Sperm and eggs produced in multicellular antheridia and archegonia, with the zygote developing into an embryo inside the archegonium
Sporangia that produce spores or seeds
Chlorophylls a and b, cellulose cell walls and a phragmoplast during cell division
clades.notes: Includes the bryophytes (mosses, liverworts, hornworts) and the vascular plants (lycophytes, ferns and horsetails, gymnosperms, angiosperms). Early evolution of the life cycle and the effect of the Devonian land plant spread on climate are covered by the literature cited. clades.name: Eukaryota
clades.sum: Organisms whose cells have a nucleus, membrane-bound organelles and a cytoskeleton: animals, plants, fungi and the many lineages of protists.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Eukaryota, unranked clade), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: DNA enclosed in a nucleus bounded by a double membrane
Membrane-bound organelles, including mitochondria derived from an engulfed alphaproteobacterium
An internal cytoskeleton of actin and microtubules
Mitosis and, in most lineages, meiosis and sexual reproduction
clades.notes: Thought to have originated in the Paleoproterozoic from a partnership between an Asgard archaeon (host) and an aerobic alphaproteobacterium that became the mitochondrion; plastids came later from cyanobacteria. The traditional four kingdoms (animals, plants, fungi, protists) are replaced in phylogenomic studies by supergroups such as Amorphea and Diphoda; protists are a paraphyletic grade. In a two-domain view the Eukaryota sit inside Archaea.

clades.name: ParaHoxozoa
clades.sum: Animals with Hox/ParaHox genes: bilaterians, cnidarians and placozoans, leaving out sponges and comb jellies.
clades.trank_src: English Wikipedia, “ParaHoxozoa”, revision 1377051484 (clade)
diag: Hox/ParaHox genes of the ANTP class, which give the group its name
Several further gene classes absent in sponges and comb jellies (among them HNF, CUT, PROS and ZF)
clades.notes: The tree node is labelled ParaHoxozoa (id kept as "eumetazoa"). If comb jellies are the first animal branch, the older name Eumetazoa is sometimes used for this same group. Whether sponges or comb jellies are the sister of all other animals is unresolved, so the base of the animal tree is shown as uncertain. A claim that sponges also have a ParaHox-like gene has been contested.

clades.name: Archaeopterygidae
clades.sum: Long-tailed, toothed early birds from the latest Jurassic and earliest Cretaceous of Europe, usually limited to Archaeopteryx and Wellnhoferia.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Archaeopterygidae, family, Huxley 1871), downloaded 2026-11-27
diag: Jaws with small teeth and a long bony tail, as in other dinosaurs of the time

clades.notes: Xu and colleagues (2011) defined the clade as all animals closer to Archaeopteryx than to the house sparrow or Dromaeosaurus. Protarchaeopteryx and Jinfengopteryx, once referred here, are now treated as an oviraptorosaur and a troodontid; Jurapteryx is probably a synonym of Archaeopteryx. A few analyses have placed Anchiornis and Xiaotingia in the family, but most later studies keep them in Anchiornithidae, and some (Hartman et al. 2019) put the archaeopterygids outside Avialae. Teeth from the Berriasian of Cherves-de-Cognac and Angeac-Charente in France are attributed to the family (Louchart et al. 2017). PBDB treats Archaeopterygidae as an invalid subgroup of Avialae; the family is kept here following the cited literature.

clades.name: Avialae
clades.sum: The clade of birds and their closest relatives, all theropods nearer to living birds than to dromaeosaurids and troodontids.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Avialae, unranked clade), downloaded 2026-11-27
diag: Feathered wings used in flapping flight (the apomorphy-based definition of Gauthier 2001)
Proatlas bones of the neck lost in most members, though still present in Archaeopteryx
clades.notes: Definitions differ. Most authors use a branch-based clade (theropods closer to birds than to Deinonychus or Dromaeosaurus); the PhyloCode definition of Benito and colleagues (2022) also excludes troodontids, and Agnolín and Novas (2013) restricted the name to the smallest clade of Archaeopteryx and modern birds. Archaeopteryx, from the Late Jurassic of Germany, is usually treated as the earliest avialan capable of powered flight, although a few analyses (Hartman et al. 2019) place it and the anchiornithids outside the group. Avialans diversified widely in the Cretaceous; teeth were lost several times independently and the bony tail was shortened to a pygostyle in Pygostylia. In this atlas the crown group (Aves, the living birds and their Mesozoic members) is kept for the Aves volumes.

clades.name: Enantiornithes
clades.sum: The "opposite birds", the most abundant and diverse avialans of the Cretaceous, mostly small, toothed and with clawed wing fingers.

Families recognised in the atlas are Pengornithidae, Longipterygidae, Bohaiornithidae and Avisauridae; most other genera are placed directly in the clade, since proposed families such as Alexornithidae, Cathayornithidae and Gobipterygidae lack consensus support.

clades.sum: The beaked, herbivorous horned-face dinosaurs of North America, Asia and Europe, from small bipedal Psittacosaurus to the huge frilled Triceratops.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Ceratopsia, suborder), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: A rostral bone, a toothless ossification at the tip of the upper jaw unique to ceratopsians, forming part of a hooked beak
Early members small and bipedal; later ones large quadrupeds with facial horns and a frill over the neck
Size from about 1 m and 23 kg to over 9 m and 9,100 kg
clades.notes: Marsh named the group in 1890. The earliest known ceratopsian, Yinlong downsi, lived about 161 to 156 million years ago in the Late Jurassic of Asia, and the last, Triceratops prorsus, died out 66 million years ago. Ceratops, which gave the group its name, is a nomen dubium. Frills may have protected the neck, served for display or thermoregulation, or anchored muscles; none of these is settled.

clades.name: Ceratopsidae
clades.sum: The large frilled and horned ceratopsians of the Late Cretaceous, mostly from western North America, including Triceratops, Centrosaurus and Styracosaurus.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Ceratopsidae, family), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: Quadrupedal herbivores with beaks and rows of shearing teeth at the back of the jaw
Elaborate nasal horns and a thin parietal-squamosal shelf extending back and up into a frill
Two subfamilies: Chasmosaurinae, with long triangular frills and large brow horns, and Centrosaurinae, with nasal horns or bosses and shorter frills
clades.notes: Marsh named the family in 1888. All but one known species come from western North America, which formed the island continent of Laramidia in most of the Late Cretaceous. Horns and frills are the main means of recognising species; their purpose is not entirely clear, and defence against predators is only one proposed use.

clades.name: Chasmosaurinae
clades.sum: The ceratopsid subfamily with prominent brow horns and long frills without long spines, species-rich in the Campanian and Maastrichtian of western North America.

Frill edges with epoccipital hornlets whose shape allows species to be told apart from fragmentary remains
clades.notes: Named by Lambe in 1915. Chasmosaurines appeared in the early Campanian and died out at the Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction. They evolved in Laramidia and are known definitively from western Canada, the western United States and northern Mexico.

clades.sum: A family of small, primitive neoceratopsians from Asia, North America and possibly Europe.

Defined as Leptoceratops gracilis and all species closer to it than to Triceratops horridus

clades.name: Marginocephalia
clades.sum: Ornithischians with a bony shelf at the back of the skull, made up of the thick-skulled pachycephalosaurs and the horned ceratopsians.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Marginocephalia, unranked clade), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: A bony shelf or margin at the back of the skull, probably used for display
Two subgroups, the thick-skulled Pachycephalosauria and the horned Ceratopsia
Primarily herbivores; basally small facultative quadrupeds, with derived members large obligate quadrupeds
clades.notes: Defined in the PhyloCode by Madzia and colleagues in 2021 by three specifiers: Ceratops montanus, Pachycephalosaurus wyomingensis and Triceratops horridus. Basal members used gastroliths to process plants, and tooth batteries evolved convergently in Neoceratopsia and Pachycephalosauria. The group arose in the Jurassic and became more common in the Cretaceous; primitive members are Asian and later forms reached North America.

clades.name: Pachycephalosauria
clades.sum: The thick-skulled, bipedal herbivores or omnivores of the Cretaceous of North America and Asia, with domed, flat or wedge-shaped skulls.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Pachycephalosauria, suborder), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: Heavily ossified, thickened skull roofs, domed, flat or wedge-shaped, with domes often ringed by nodes or spikes
Bipedal build with short forelimbs, long legs, a short thick neck and a heavy tail
Large orbits and a large optic nerve, pointing to good vision
clades.notes: Named by Maryańska and Osmólska in 1974. No complete skeleton is known, and isolated skull fragments are often all that is found. The oldest definite pachycephalosaur is Zavacephale from the Early Cretaceous of Mongolia; earlier candidates such as Stenopelix, which a 2017 analysis placed in Ceratopsia, are doubted.

clades.name: Protoceratopsidae
clades.sum: Small basal ceratopsians from the Late Cretaceous of Asia, mostly China and Mongolia, with a modest frill and no large horns.

An unusually small antorbital fenestra, with the antorbital fossa high on the skull joined by a slit to a maxillary sinus unique to the family
Body length of about 1 to 2.5 m, with a frill and horns much smaller than in ceratopsids
clades.notes: Granger and Gregory named it in 1923. Protoceratopsids had constantly replaced tooth batteries for slicing plants and a hooked beak, and may have had cheeks.

clades.name: Psittacosauridae
clades.sum: The Early Cretaceous Asian family of bipedal, parrot-beaked ceratopsians centred on Psittacosaurus.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Psittacosauridae, family), downloaded 2026-11-16

Early members of the ceratopsian line, though closer to Triceratops than Yinlong
Known from Asia, with the close relative Aquilops from North America
clades.notes: Osborn created the family in 1923 for Psittacosaurus, which he thought might be related to Ankylosauria. Hongshanosaurus, once placed here as a separate genus, is now regarded as a junior synonym of Psittacosaurus, and the family is considered an early offshoot of the line leading to derived ceratopsians.

clades.name: Ornithischia
clades.sum: Extinct, mainly herbivorous dinosaurs with a bird-like, backward-pointing pubis, ranging from small early runners to armoured, horned and duck-billed giants.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Ornithischia, unranked clade), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: A predentary bone at the tip of the lower jaw and a palpebral bone above the eye
An opisthopubic pubis (pointing backward along the ischium), an increased number of sacral vertebrae and no gastralia
Early members about 1 to 2 m long and bipedal, with forelimbs much shorter than hindlimbs
clades.notes: Named by Seeley in 1888 for the “bird-hipped” pelvis, although birds descend from theropods and are only distantly related to the group. Ornithischians include the armoured Thyreophora, the horned and thick-skulled Marginocephalia and the Ornithopoda, found on every continent; some lineages are known from filament-like integument (Tianyulong, Psittacosaurus, Kulindadromeus). The placement of Heterodontosauria and of several early forms (Lesothosaurus, Eocursor, Laquintasaura, Pisanosaurus) is unsettled among recent analyses, so these sit directly in Ornithischia, marked incertae sedis where analyses disagree.

clades.name: Ankylopollexia
clades.sum: Thumb-spiked iguanodontians of the Late Jurassic to the end of the Cretaceous, from Camptosaurus to the duck-billed hadrosaurs.

clades.name: Dryosauridae
clades.sum: Fast-running, bipedal herbivorous ornithopods of the Middle Jurassic to Early Cretaceous of Africa, Europe and North America.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Dryosauridae, family), downloaded 2026-11-16

Fossil record from the Middle Jurassic to the Early Cretaceous in Africa, Europe and North America, perhaps extending to other southern continents

clades.name: Hadrosauridae
clades.sum: The duck-billed dinosaurs, herbivorous ornithopods with dental batteries that dominated Late Cretaceous Asia and North America.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Hadrosauridae, family), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: Teeth stacked into complex dental batteries that formed grinding surfaces
Predentary bone and a backward-pointing pubis, as in other ornithischians
Facultative bipeds: young of some species walked mostly on two legs, adults mostly on four

Hadrosaurids descend from Late Jurassic or Early Cretaceous iguanodontians and spread in the last stage of the Cretaceous to Europe, Africa, South America and possibly Antarctica.

Defined under the PhyloCode (Madzia et al. 2021) as the smallest clade containing Dryosaurus altus, Iguanodon bernissartensis, Rhabdodon priscus and Tenontosaurus tilletti, provided it does not include Hypsilophodon foxii
clades.notes: Sereno defined it in 1998 as the most inclusive group containing Parasaurolophus walkeri but not Hypsilophodon foxii; the 2021 definition limits it to its traditionally included species. English Wikipedia lists it as an infraorder within a suborder Ornithopoda, whereas Benton (2004) treats Ornithopoda as an infraorder and does not rank Iguanodontia. The traditional Iguanodontoidea and Iguanodontidae are a paraphyletic grade leading to the hadrosaurs, so many of their genera now sit in Hadrosauroidea.

clades.name: Iguanodontidae
clades.sum: Large iguanodontians of the Early Cretaceous, the family of Iguanodon, whose monophyly is disputed.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Iguanodontidae, family, Bonaparte 1850), downloaded 2026-11-25
diag: Elongated maxillae, a convex skull roof and a reduced antorbital fenestra
Hoof-like second, third and fourth digits, in some a specialised thumb spike; both bipedal and quadrupedal locomotion are evidenced
clades.notes: Defined under the PhyloCode (Madzia et al. 2021) as the largest clade containing Iguanodon bernissartensis but not Hadrosaurus foulkii. There is no consensus on its phylogeny: it is most often found paraphyletic with respect to Hadrosauridae, although some researchers argue for monophyly. PBDB lists Bolong and Barilium in it but puts Iguanodon itself directly in Ankylopollexia; here Iguanodon, the type genus, sits in it by definition, and Bolong, which English Wikipedia calls a basal hadrosauroid, sits in Styracosterna as incertae sedis.

clades.name: Ornithopoda
clades.sum: Herbivorous ornithischians from small bipedal runners to large duck-billed forms, found worldwide and most diverse in the Cretaceous.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Ornithopoda, suborder), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: Birdlike feet; no body armour; an elongated pubis; no mandibular fenestra in the lower jaw
Primitive members small and bipedal, derived Iguanodontia larger and facultatively or obligately quadrupedal
A chewing apparatus that became the most elaborate of any non-avian dinosaur, peaking in the hadrosaurids
clades.notes: Named by Marsh in 1881 for the “bird feet” of its members. Early members were about a metre long; the largest, such as Shantungosaurus, reached about 15 m and roughly 23 tonnes. The old family Hypsilophodontidae is a paraphyletic grade, not a clade, so small bipedal neornithischians are placed by recent analyses rather than lumped here. Dental microwear suggests early members browsed and derived iguanodontians fed in bulk on tougher plants. Part of this volume sits in the clades below; genera whose position among them is disputed are marked incertae sedis within Ornithopoda.

clades.name: Rhabdodontomorpha
clades.sum: Early-diverging iguanodontians of Europe and Gondwana, from small to large plant eaters, including the rhabdodontids and the muttaburrasaurids.

Tenontosaurus and its relatives have been recovered tentatively as basal members, a North American radiation; the more inclusive Rhabdodontoidea was named by Poole in 2022. The lineage probably split from other iguanodontians in the Middle Jurassic.

clades.name: Sauropoda
clades.sum: The giant long-necked, four-legged plant-eaters, which include the largest animals that ever lived on land.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Sauropoda, unranked clade), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: Very long neck and tail with a small head compared with the body

Some members reached enormous size; the group includes the largest known land animals
clades.notes: Named by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1878. Sauropod-like tracks from the Late Triassic of Greenland may point to an earlier origin. By the Late Jurassic, about 150 million years ago, sauropods were widespread.

clades.name: Sauropodomorpha
clades.sum: The long-necked, plant-eating dinosaurs, from small Triassic bipeds to the giant sauropods, and their kin.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Sauropodomorpha, unranked clade), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: Saurischian dinosaurs that include the sauropods and the early forms once grouped as "prosauropods"
The earliest members were small bipeds of 1–2 m that ate meat or a mixed diet, and herbivory soon became the rule
A trend towards larger body size, longer necks and quadrupedal posture, ending in the sauropods
clades.notes: Named by Friedrich von Huene in 1932, who split it into the basal Prosauropoda and the giant Sauropoda. Analyses since the 2000s place Sauropoda inside a paraphyletic "Prosauropoda", so that name is no longer used as a natural group; the early forms are placed in several families that arose from one lineage. Sauropodomorpha is the sister group of Theropoda within Saurischia, although a small minority of authors have grouped it with Ornithischia. The oldest known members come from the Late Triassic Ischigualasto Formation, and the group ended with the non-avian dinosaurs 66 million years ago. Remains are known from every continent, including Antarctica.

clades.name: Ankylosauria
clades.sum: Heavily armoured, bulky quadrupedal herbivores covered in bony osteoderms, known from the Middle Jurassic to the end of the Cretaceous.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Ankylosauria, unranked clade), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: Small and large bony shields fused together to cover the back and sides, fused to the skull bones on the head
Bulky quadrupeds with short, powerful limbs
Dorsal ribs that fit snugly against the vertebrae
clades.notes: Named by Osborn in 1923, and usually ranked as a suborder or infraorder in Linnaean schemes. The two main families, Nodosauridae and Ankylosauridae, are mainly from the Northern Hemisphere; the more basal Parankylosauria are known from Cretaceous southern Gondwana, though they may instead be a separate lineage of thyreophorans outside Ankylosauria and Stegosauria. A 2023 review rejects the traditional Ankylosauridae-Nodosauridae split and refers the nodosaurids to three families: Panoplosauridae, Polacanthidae and Struthiosauridae. The group is thought to have first appeared in North Africa in the Middle Jurassic.

An S-shaped narial passage
clades.notes: Barnum Brown named the family and the subfamily Ankylosaurinae in 1908, after Ankylosaurus was found in Montana in 1906. The oldest known members date to about 122 million years ago and the family ended at the Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction. They were obligate quadrupeds with leaf-shaped teeth and are known only from the Northern Hemisphere.

clades.name: Nodosauridae
clades.sum: The club-less armoured ankylosaurs of the Late Jurassic to Late Cretaceous of Asia, Europe and North America, often with spikes on the shoulders.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Nodosauridae, family), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: No mace-like tail club; the tail tip stayed more flexible
Rows of bony armour nodules and spines (osteoderms) covered in keratin sheaths, often with shoulder spines projecting outward
clades.notes: Marsh erected the family in 1890 on the genus Nodosaurus. Sereno defined it in 1998 as the ankylosaurs closer to Panoplosaurus than to Ankylosaurus. Some analyses recover it as a paraphyletic grade leading to the ankylosaurids, and a 2023 review splits it into several families (see Ankylosauria). The Borealopelta holotype preserves armour in life position with skin and keratin showing a reddish, countershaded pattern.

clades.name: Stegosauria
clades.sum: Plated, herbivorous ornithischians of the Jurassic and Early Cretaceous, known from the Northern Hemisphere, Africa and South America, with dorsal plates and paired tail spikes.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Stegosauria, unranked clade), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: Quadrupedal herbivores with large, thin, erect dermal plates along the neck, back and tail
Pairs of spikes at the end of the tail (the thagomizer), used as a defensive weapon
Small, long, flat and narrow head with a horn-covered beak over the premaxillae and predentary
clades.notes: Named by Marsh in 1877 and made up of two families, the Huayangosauridae and the more diverse Stegosauridae. The earliest unequivocal stegosaurians come from the Middle Jurassic (Bajocian-Bathonian) and include Adratiklit, Bashanosaurus, Isaberrysaura and Thyreosaurus. The function of the plates (defence, thermoregulation or display) is still debated; a histological study suggests the plates served different purposes at different life stages.

clades.name: Thyreophora
clades.sum: The armoured ornithischians, carrying rows of keeled bony scutes along the body from the Early Jurassic to the end of the Cretaceous, made up of the stegosaurs, the ankylosaurs and their early relatives.
clades.trank_src: Paleobiology Database taxonomy (taxon Thyreophora, unranked clade), downloaded 2026-11-16
diag: Osteoderms (bony growths in the skin) with lateral keels, lined up in longitudinal rows along the body
Skull and jaw characters including a wide jugal, remodelled dermal skull bone and a down-turned dentary tooth row
Fore limbs much shorter than the hindlimbs; stegosaurs and ankylosaurs were obligate quadrupeds, whereas the early Scutellosaurus was probably mostly bipedal
clades.notes: Named by Nopcsa in 1915 and defined as a clade by Sereno in 1998 as the genasaurs closer to Ankylosaurus than to Triceratops. It is the sister group of Cerapoda within Genasauria. Most authors keep it unranked, with Stegosauria and Ankylosauria as its two major subgroups, though it is sometimes treated as a suborder. Early members such as Scutellosaurus and Scelidosaurus have simple, low, keeled scutes; later forms evolved spikes and plates.

home.title: Life on Earth
home.lead: Every organism in this atlas — from bacteria to pterosaurs — belongs to one family tree that goes back more than three and a half billion years.
intro: Earth is about 4.54 billion years old, and life appeared early in its history: the oldest fossils that clearly record living things are stromatolites about 3.48 billion years old from the Dresser Formation of Western Australia. Older traces, chemical signals in rocks and crystals, may push the start back to 3.7 or even 4.1 billion years.

All living things share the same genetic code and the same molecular machinery for building proteins, which is why biologists accept that they descend from a single last universal common ancestor (LUCA). From it come three great lineages of cells: Bacteria, Archaea and eukaryotes — the organisms whose cells have a nucleus. Current evidence places the origin of eukaryotes inside the archaea, from a host related to today's Asgard archaea that took in a bacterium; the tree of this atlas follows that view.

For most of this history life was microscopic. Animals with complex bodies diversified rapidly from about 539 million years ago, in the Cambrian explosion, and the living world has since been reshaped by five major mass extinctions. The groups below give a glimpse of that diversity; each picture opens its place in the tree.
